div.head: List of Papers
div.p: [Incoming papers are listed chronologically under date of receipt. Unless otherwise specified, the correspondence is from or to officials in the Department of State.]
PART I: THE CONTINUATION AND CONCLUSION OF THE—WARPARTICIPATION OF THE UNITED STATES

p.hi: The Conduct of the War—Discussions of Peace and Conclusion of the Armistices

speeches on war aims by the british prime minister, january 5, and by president wilson (the fourteen points), january 8; comment in associated and enemy countries-speech of the french minister of foreign affairs, january 13—unofficial austro-german advances regarding peace to the american professor herron

row.cell: British inquiry regarding Bulgaria’s attitude toward separate peace. Chargé suggests offering opportunity for statement.
Department approves of offering Bulgarian representatives opportunity to state attitude on separate peace.
Teutonic peace offensive. Reported conditions of peace.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Prime Minister’s speech of Jan. 5 on war aims is expression of British opinion.
Speech on war aims before Trade Union Conference at London.
Speech on war aims, delivered at joint session of Congress; program of fourteen points as peace conditions.
Italian press comment on Lloyd George’s speech of Jan. 5.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Laudatory editorials on the President’s speech of Jan. 8. General depression dissipated.
Foreign Minister’s comments on the President’s message of Jan. 8.
French people receive President Wilson’s message of Jan. 8 with gratitude. Press comment.
Substance of Herron’s letter on Austro-German unofficial advances regarding peace.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Inquires reaction of German Liberals to the President’s statement of peace terms.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on the President’s speech of Jan. 8.
Italian press comment on the President’s speech.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Statement of German Moderate views on peace program as proclaimed by President Wilson.
Quotes Foreign Minister’s speech opposing international workingmen’s conference and defining French war aims.
Peace proposals should be made through official channels. Position taken by Herron is approved.
From the Ambassador in France (tel.); to House also
Plans for forming general reserve under Supreme War Council to be kept at disposal of commanders in chief.
From the Consul General at London
Transmits statement of British Labor organizations approving the President’s speech of Jan. 8.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Czernin reported to have pronounced as sound some of the fourteen clauses of the President’s speech.
Italy criticizes Lloyd George’s speech and asserts right to territory on eastern coast of Adriatic.
Italy demands Trieste and other parts of eastern Adriatic coast.
From the Minister in Sweden (tel.): to the President
Czernin represented as being in accord with views expressed in the President’s message of Jan. 8.
Conclusions reached by military representatives of Supreme War Council regarding war situation and 1918 campaign.
Resolution of military representatives of Supreme War Council urging formation of general reserve. Committee of supply created.

p.hi: speeches of the german chancellor (hertling) and the austro-hungarian minister of foreign affairs (czernin), january 24

row.cell: From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Hertling’s address to Reichstag Committee in reply to President Wilson and Lloyd George.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.); similar tel. to the Minister in Switzerland
Instructions to cable comments of German Socialist and Liberal papers on Hertling’s address.
Italian officials seek reaffirmation of secret treaty between Italy, France, England, and Russia, recently published.
Reply to French inquiry regarding meaning of point 10 of the President’s address of Jan. 8.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
British press comment on German Chancellor’s speech of Jan. 24.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on the Chancellor’s speech of Jan. 24.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Reported that Hertling and Czernin conferred together before making their speeches.
General strike in Austria, press account of which was suppressed in Germany, an evidence of dissension between two powers.
German press comment on the Chancellor’s speech of Jan. 24.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Hertling states public opinion demands restoration of German colonies for liberation of Belgium.
Request that small Allied states be represented at peace conference. Restoration of Greek nationals desired.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to repeat to Ambassadors in France and Italy
Press report untrue that Czernin’s speech was submitted to President Wilson before being delivered.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Rumor of peace negotiations between Austria and the United States believed to be another move in German peace offensive.
Czernin’s speech of Jan. 24 on Russian peace and general peace negotiations.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Report that Reichstag deems declaration as to Belgium inadvisable. Offer of secret peace negotiations with the United States.
Italy satisfied that Great Britain will observe secret treaty.
Lammasch sends message to President Wilson regarding willingness of Emperor Charles to make separate peace with Allies.

p.hi: third session of the supreme war council, january 30—february 21 discussion of the use of american troops-public statement of the allied premiers denouncing the enemy peace program-objection by the united states to collective pronouncements by the supreme war council,—unofficial conversations on peace between professor herron and a bulgarian emissary

row.cell: From the Ambassador in France (tel.); to House also
Frazier reports Supreme War Council’s discussion of amalgamation of U.S. troops in French or British divisions.
From the Ambassador in France (tel.); to House also
Frazier reports discussion of use of U.S. troops; Pershing’s objections to British plan and his counter-proposition.
Unofficial conversations between Herron and Bulgarian emissary on peace and on Bulgaria’s aims.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); similar tel. to the Ambassadors in France and Italy
Informal assurance that no peace negotiations will be entered into without knowledge of Allies.
Papal effort to bring belligerents together. President Wilson requested to make statement.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on strike movement, Socialist attitude, etc.
Frazier’s report: Public statement of Supreme War Council regarding continuation of war.
Suggests withholding answer to Czernin until receipt of telegram now being prepared.
Instructions to withhold from French and British chiefs of mission information of Austrian offer of separate peace.
From the Consul General at London
Transmits Prime Minister’s speech of Jan. 18 on continuation of the war and interpellations of Trade Union delegates.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
The United States will enter into no secret negotiations with representatives of German Government.
To the Ambassador in France (tel.): to Frazier
Objection to issuance of collective statements by Supreme War Council unless submitted for approval of President Wilson.
Desires to inform British and French missions that Austrian peace conversations are being discussed with their Governments from Washington.

p.hi: the herron-lammasch conversations, february 3–4

row.cell: Report of conversations of Herron and Lammasch at Berne, and Herron’s interview with Muehlon.
Political and economic situation in Germany and Austria; Bohemian independence movement.
Opinion divided regarding powers of Supreme War Council, yet confidence felt in strength of military situation.

p.hi: president Wilson’s speech in reply to hertling and czernin, february 11; comment in associated and enemy countries-assurances transmitted to lammasch, february 15–letter of emperor charles to president wilson, february 17

row.cell: Speech on peace terms delivered at joint session of Congress in reply to Hertling and Czernin.
Favorable comment of Rome press on President Wilson’s address of Feb. 11. Address of Premier.
French official endorsement of, and press comment on, President Wilson’s speech of Feb. 11.
Publication of secret treaty of 1915. Declarations in Chamber of Deputies on Italy’s claims.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on President Wilson’s speech of Feb. 11.
Instruction to convey secret, unofficial assurance to Austria of U.S. financial aid in case of breach with Germany.
Emperor Charles’s declaration to Austrian people on Ukraine peace.
Further comment by German press on President Wilson’s speech of Feb. 11.
Foreign Minister discusses U. S. participation in the war, Vatican position on peace moves, and clause 15 of secret treaty.
Interview between Haussmann of Liberal Populist Party and Herron regarding the President’s message.
Austrian official asks whether the United States would help Austria break with Germany and make separate peace.
Vienna press comment on President Wilson’s speech of Feb. 11.
To the Ambassador in France (tel.); the same to the Ambassadors in Great Britain and Italy
The President disapproves of actions of Supreme War Council and Inter-Allied Board regarding political subjects.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); mutatis mutandis, to the Ambassador in France
Venizelos desires statement from the Allies of intention to protect rights of Greece. Instruction to inquire British attitude.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Text of Austro-Hungarian secret message to Spain to be forwarded to President Wilson, proposing negotiations for peace.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Evidence that Austrian Emperor’s peace message to President Wilson is sent with approval of Germany.
Suggestion that larger number of officers be sent in military mission to Italy.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Communications between Czernin and Austro-Hungarian Ambassador at Madrid regarding secret peace message to President Wilson.
Department’s secret message transmitted to Lammasch at Vienna.
From the Vice Consul at Zurich (tel.)
German offensive being held back in hope that President Wilson’s attitude may open way for peace.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Germany believed to be inclined to make statement concerning restoration of Belgium.
From the Vice Consul at Zurich (tel.)
Reported statements of Hertling and others regarding disposal of Belgium, Alsace-Lorraine, etc.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Interview with Clemenceau on President Wilson’s objection to collective announcements of Supreme War Council.
Political situation in Germany; reform bills.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
British Government prepared to join in statement of intention to protect rights of Greece.

p.hi: chancellor hertling’s speech, february 25—british attitude toward german and austrian advances regarding peace-support by the united states of proposals for an inter-allied general reserve-italian request for american troops

row.cell: From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Transmits substance of Hertling’s speech in Reichstag regarding German war aims.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Message of Austro-Hungarian Ambassador in Spain to Czernin on delivery of secret peace message to Spanish King.
Reported that Germany seeks understanding with President Wilson for bringing about peace.
France would take up with President Wilson secret proposals for peace which the Central Powers are making.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Balfour’s comments on Austrian peace advances to the United States.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Quotes from Balfour’s speech in House of Commons on futility of beginning peace negotiations at present.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Inquiry regarding results of Inter-Allied Labor Conference at London and views of delegates who will visit the United States.
France is disposed to offer protection to Greece.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Memorandum on war aims of Inter-Allied Labor and Socialist Conference is being sent by pouch.
Belgium will discuss peace only in concert with its allies.
Press comment on twofold aim of Hertling’s speech. Account of speeches of Payer and Scheidemann on party issues.
Bulgarian unofficial advance regarding separate peace. Instructions requested.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Spanish King informs Austrian Emperor that his peace message has been delivered to President Wilson.
Excerpts from speech of Lammasch before Austrian Upper House on peace negotiations and Austrian policy.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Reports British views on resolutions of Inter-Allied Labor Conference at London. Delegates to the United States being chosen.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
U.S. support of proposals for inter-Allied general reserve.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Personnel of proposed Socialist mission to the United States.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Inquiry regarding British participation in Stockholm Conference, and regarding secret proposals submitted to Labor Party and Socialist Conference.

p.hi: memorandum of the inter-allied labor and socialist conference on war aims, february 23 (received march 18)—proposals for a discussion between socialist and labor parties of the allied and central powers and for an allied socialist mission to the united states; attitude of the american government—allied reverses in france: american assurances of reenforcements—communications exchanged between president wilson and emperor Charles—the american labor mission to europe

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Great Britain
Transmits memorandum on war aims adopted Feb. 23 by Inter-Allied Labor and Socialist Conference at London.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Reported discussion by British and Italian officials of article 15 of secret treaty.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); the same to the Ambassador in France
Approval of resolutions of Supreme War Council regarding inter-Allied general reserve.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
British attitude toward Socialist conference of delegates from belligerent countries.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.); to the President also
Allied Governments disapprove of conference of Socialists of Allied and Central Powers, but approve of Allied Socialist mission to the United States.
To the Ambassador in France (tel.); the same to the Ambassadors in Great Britain and Italy
Opposed to unofficial international conferences such as proposed by Socialist and Labor Parties.
Inquires if Department desires any reply given to unofficial Bulgarian representative.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.): to the President
British defeat in France; desperate need of men.
Report of German ultimatum to Austria as result of Lammasch’s negotiations in Switzerland.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Meaning of article 15 of secret treaty between Great Britain and Italy, inaccurately revealed by Russian Maximalists.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
The United States is urged to rush further military reenforcements to France.
French approval of exposition of U.S. attitude toward unofficial international conferences.
Military situation in France as described by Foreign Minister.
Foreign Minister in full accord with U. S. views regarding unofficial international conferences.
The Secretary of War to President Wilson (tel.)
Military situation in France and disposition of U.S. troops at front.
To the Ambassador in France (tel.): House to Frazier
The President deems it inexpedient for special mission representing any party to visit the United States at present.
The Secretary of War to President Wilson (tel.)
Recommends temporary augmentation of Allied forces by U.S. infantry but their ultimate reincorporation under U.S. command.
The Military Representative, Supreme War Council, to The Adjutant General (tel.)
Joint note of the military representatives of Supreme War Council on U.S. replacements, transmitted for action by the President.
The British Ambassador on Special Mission to President Wilson
Presents Lloyd George’s telegram of Mar. 28 on military crisis and necessity for coordination of forces under General Foch.
Italian plea for small American force in Italy for moral effect.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Quotes Spanish King’s message of Mar. 5 to Emperor Charles when communicating President Wilson’s reply to secret peace proposals.
It is desired that conditions as basis for general peace be explicitly stated.
Further statement of views regarding bases of peace.
The Adjutant General to the Military Representative, Supreme War Council (tel.): to Baker
Authorization to decide questions of immediate cooperation or replacement.
No special message for Bulgaria. Joint effort with Austria toward peace suggested.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Lloyd George thinks that present battle will probably lead to appointment of an executive generalissimo.
From the British Ambassador on Special Mission
Conveys expression of thanks from Lloyd George to the President for assurances of prompt reenforcements.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); mutatis mutandis, to the Ambassadors in France and Italy
Contrary to U.S. policy to discuss international questions with citizens of foreign state unless by authority of their government.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Requests courtesy for delegation of American Federation of Labor, which seeks to cooperate with U.S. and Allied Governments.

p.hi: speech of the austro-hungarian minister of foreign affairs (czernin), april 2—request of the greek government for guarantees

row.cell: From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Quotes address of Czernin to delegation of Common Council of Vienna on political situation, appealing for united effort in war.
Visit of U.S. Secretary of War to Italy. Importance of presence of U.S. military force for moral effect.
Presents Greek message to the President requesting assurances regarding territorial integrity of Greece.
The Secretary of War to President Wilson (tel.)
Estimate of German strength; U.S. troops facing action; supreme command given Foch.
Clemenceau looks upon U.S. attitude toward Socialist Conference as vindication of his position.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.): Hurley to Stevens
Program to meet call of Supreme War Council for fullest possible immediate military participation.
Transfer of U.S. ambulance sections to Italy for duty with Italian forces.

p.hi: president wilson’s speech of april 6; comment in associated and enemy countries—assurances to greece, april 19

row.cell: Speech made at Baltimore on anniversary of entering war and in interest of Liberty Loan.
Peace feelers by Austria-Hungary apparently designed to provoke the United States into taking ostensible initiative.
French official commendation of President Wilson’s speech of Apr. 6, and press comment.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); to the President also
Appreciation expressed in Great Britain for hastening of U.S. troops to Europe. The President’s Baltimore speech commended.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on President Wilson’s speech of Apr. 6.
Foreign Minister desires to communicate to Parliament U.S. declaration of policy regarding unofficial conferences.
Report of the Consul at Paris
Pacifism and popular unrest in France.
Reports progress of great battle in north and publication of letter of Emperor Charles to Prince Sixte de Bourbon.
Effect in France of publication by Clemenceau of letter of Emperor Charles to Prince Sixte de Bourbon.
No objection to use in Parliament of U.S. declaration of policy regarding unofficial conferences.
Bulgaria seeks friendly support in Balkans; advances unheeded by Greece.
From the British Ambassador on Special Mission
French Government agrees that General Foch be designated commander in chief of Allied armies in France.
Informal assurances of assistance in preserving integrity of Greece. The President’s note of Apr. 5 to Venizelos quoted.
Herron approached by German pacifists asserting Germany ready for negotiations.
Effect of U.S. assurances to Greece.
Possibility of German secret official proposals of peace conversations with Entente.

p.hi: fifth session of the supreme war council, may 1–21 discussion of the use of american troops—consideration’ of the advisability of declaring a state of war with turkey and Bulgaria—president wilson’s speech of may 18

row.cell: From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Discussion in fifth session of Supreme War Council of allotment of U.S. troops.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Agreement reached in Supreme War Council on subject of employment of U.S. troops.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); the same to the Ambassadors in France and Italy
Inquires attitude of Government to which accredited toward U.S. declaration of war with Turkey and/or Bulgaria.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Executive War Board superseded by supreme commander by agreement of Beauvais.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Discussion of Beauvais agreement and Italian reenforcements for France.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Further discussions in Supreme War Council on disposition of U.S. troops, Pershing insisting on independent U.S. Army.
U.S. declaration of war upon Turkey and Bulgaria recommended by Italy.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Criticism of agreement of Abbeville and plan advocated by Pershing.
Pichon will bring before Council of Ministers the U.S. proposal of declaration of war on Turkey and Bulgaria.
From the Ambassador in France (tel.): from Bliss
Joint recommendation of military representatives, Supreme War Council, on subject of U.S. declaration of war on Turkey and Bulgaria.
From the Vice Consul at Zurich (tel.)
German Chancellor secretly offers to open negotiations with the United States for exchange of peace ideas.
France considers U.S. declaration of war on Turkey and Bulgaria as desirable.
Favorable reception accorded American Labor Commission in Paris.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.); the same to the Ambassador in France
The United States will redouble its efforts to assist Italy in prosecution of the war against the Central Powers.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press summary of meeting of German and Austrian Emperors at Spa.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Quotes Foreign Office note of May 17: Great Britain considers it desirable that the United States declare war on Turkey and Bulgaria. Reasons.
Speech opening campaign in New York for the second Red Cross fund.
Report of the Special Agent at Cairo
Political situation in Syria; ambitions of the King of the Hejaz.
To the Minister in Sweden (tel.); similar tel. to the Ambassador in Great Britain
Requests report on Stockholm Conference of 1917, especially on relations between German Socialists and Bolsheviks.
Stockholm conference never took place. Certain delegates presented reports to Dutch-Scandinavian Committee or conferred with German Socialists.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on President Wilson’s speech of May 18.
Report of the Special Agent at Cairo
Growing discontent among Arabs; reasons therefor. Speeches on British and French policies.

p.hi: sixth session of the supreme war council, june 1–3: the question of unity of naval command in the mediterranean—appeal of the allied premiers for more american troops—fresh reverses in france—assurances to france and promise of american troops to Italy—“peace offensive” in the german press—speeches of kühlmann and hertling, june 24 and 25—change of government in bulgaria: unofficial advances regarding peace

row.cell: From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Subject of supreme command in Mediterranean taken up in sixth session of Supreme War Council.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Supreme War Council agrees upon unity of command in Mediterranean, Adriatic, and Aegean.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Resolution of unity of command withdrawn as Italian representative insists upon Italy’s command in Adriatic.
Press reports resolutions of German Social Democratic Labor Party at Vienna and terms of peace Central Powers are urged to offer.
The Allied Prime Ministers to President Wilson (tel.)
General Pershing to The Adjutant General (tel.): to Baker and March
Text of agreement with French and British for transportation of U.S. troops in June and July.
From the Chargé in Great Britain (tel.)
Prospects of an international Socialist conference.
From the British Ambassador on Special Mission
Instructions given British delegate to prisoner-of-war conference in case of German approach on subject of peace.
Comment on German press suggestion of a peace offensive consisting of publication of German war aims.
Second offensive in France checked. Precautions taken in defense of Paris; confidence in U.S. troops.
Sending of U.S. troops to Italy favorably considered.
Expression of appreciation of U.S. participation in the war.
U.S. troops will be sent to Italy.
Assurance of adequate support for France.
Report of German political situation. Program of war aims as press suggestion.
To the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Explanation requested of Bulgaria for placing its officers on enemy submarines engaged in active aggression against the United States.
From the Chargé in Great Britain (tel.)
U.S. Labor delegates fail to accord with views of British and French Socialists. British Labor conference to be held.
From the Vice Consul at Zurich (tel.)
Reliable information received that Germany is anxious to make peace on a status quo ante basis.
Criticism of America and lack of cooperation reported from Italy. Instructions to make statement of U.S. attitude.
No criticism of America since war with Austria was declared by the United States.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Substance of Kühlmann’s speech before Reichstag: War situation and prospect of peace.
Bulgaria’s unofficial advances regarding peace. Recommendations.
Italian attitude toward proposed single commander of all Allied naval forces.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Speech of Hertling, June 25, on foreign policies.
Bulgarian aspirations unofficially communicated to British representative. Change in government.
Germany sending agents to prepare way for conciliatory peace in case offensive in France fails.
Instructions to report activities of Bulgarians but to abstain from conversations with them or with Turks.
Kühlmann’s statement in favor of diplomatic discussions to aid in bringing about peace arouses anger of Conservatives.

p.hi: president wilson’s speech of july 4—seventh session of the supreme war council, july 2–4—the herron-de fiori conversations

row.cell: Address delivered at Mount Vernon, restating peace principles.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Discussion in Supreme War Council of means of supplying tonnage for transportation of U.S. troops.
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.)
Termination of seventh session of Council. Text of public announcement.
Summary of Scheidemann’s Reichstag speech commenting on Kühlmann’s utterances.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
German press comment on President Wilson’s speech of July 4.
De Fiori again interviews Herron, bringing tentative peace program from Bavaria.
From the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Bulgaria desires friendly relations with the United States. Denies hostile acts of Bulgarians.
From the Consul General at London
Transmits copies of Balfour’s speech in House of Commons, June 20, on subject of peace by negotiation.
Eastern question not dealt with in Bavarian tentative peace program, hence latter not acceptable.
To the Minister in Switzerland (tel.): Harrison to Wilson
Instructions to try to win over Arab commission, sent to Switzerland to promote German and Turkish propaganda.
Unofficial report that Bulgarian Army desires to cooperate with Balkan neighbors and Entente against Germany.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Text of Hertling’s speech in the Reichstag on foreign and domestic policy and willingness for peace.
Text of Herron’s note inquiring if the President desires that he make any reply to Bavarian advances.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Hertling’s remarks in the Reichstag on future of Belgium.
Effect of assassination of German Ambassador in Russia. Resignation of Kühlmann. Ludendorff’s policy.
Requests permission to inform British, French, and Italian colleagues of De Fiori’s communications.
No objection to informing British, French, and Italian colleagues of De Fiori’s communications.
Unofficial German advances toward Belgium regarding peace.
From the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
Bulgarian note stating Bulgarian officers training in Germany not authorized to take part in hostilities against America.
Message for Herron regarding Bavarian peace advances.
British official, Geneva, has taken up with his Government question of giving financial support to Bulgarian Revolutionary Party.
Bavarian peace program to be revised. Secret communication with President Wilson desired by Germany.
Regret of Liberals at Kühlmann’s resignation. Chancellor’s concessions to Socialists. Belgium held as pledge.
From the Diplomatic Agent at Cairo (tel.)
Reports use of U.S. flag in Egypt by American Jewish battalion joining British forces for service in Palestine.
From the Consul General at Sofia
Friendly feeling of new Bulgarian Cabinet for the United States.
From the Vice Consul at Zurich (tel.)
Hertling’s acceptance of peace conditions of President Wilson’s Mount Vernon speech, transmitted through unofficial channels.
Protest against Bulgarian action and request that Serbia be permitted to participate in negotiations concerning its future.
To the Diplomatic Agent at Cairo (tel.)
Instructions to make representations to British authorities and Jewish battalion against display of U.S. flag in Egypt and Palestine.
Instruction to inform Italy that the United States supports proposal for unity of command in the Mediterranean.
Belgium declines to consider Germany’s peace advances.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (tel.)
Effect of publication in Germany of news of military reverses.
Herron instructed to reply to De Fiori that the United States will consider only official communications regarding peace.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
British Labor Party protests against Government’s refusal of passports to attend neutral conference.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Gompers’ visit hailed as antidote to pacifism which is causing division in British Labor Party.
To the Minister in the Netherlands
From the Diplomatic Liaison Officer, Supreme War Council (tel.); to House also
Pershing proposes united action on all fronts to end war, and suggests that this be urged by President Wilson.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Depression in Germany. Fulfillment of royal proclamation on equal suffrage urged. Bavarian resentment against economic arrangement.
German unofficial offer of conditional independence to Belgium.
German offer to Belgium does not merit favorable consideration.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Summary of Payer’s speech at Stuttgart on peace terms.

p.hi: austro-hungarian peace note, september 16; american reply, september 17—hertling’s speech, september 24

row.cell: Communicates Austro-Hungarian message to Sweden for transmission to belligerent states, proposing conference to discuss peace terms.
The President replies that peace terms have already been stated and declines to consider conference.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
U.S. reply to Austrian peace proposal accords with British views.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Press universally approves the President’s answer to Austrian note.
Political discussion in Germany revolves around subject of peace. Criticism of Austrian peace note.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Text of German reply to Austrian peace note: Germany is prepared to participate in proposed peace conference.
To the Minister in Switzerland (tel.): to Garrett
Cautions against entertaining German or Austrian overtures for peace during prisoner-of-war conferences.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Possible British attempt to detach Turkey from Central Powers as result of successes in Palestine.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Hertling’s speech before Main Committee of Reichstag on seriousness of situation and German attitude.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
No evidence that Great Britain is considering separate peace with Turkey.

p.hi: president Wilson’s speech of September 27—the Bulgarian armistice september 29—declaration of the united states against a separate peace with bulgaria, october 2—replacement of chancellor hertling by prince max of baden

row.cell: To the diplomatic representatives in Allied and Associated countries (tel.)
Forwards copies of President Wilson’s address of Sept. 27 with request for expression of opinion thereon by government to which accredited.
Speech at New York opening campaign for Fourth Liberty Loan: further statement on war issues.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Bulgarian note of Sept. 26 will be sent to Department for such action as it may consider appropriate.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Text of Bulgarian note of Sept. 26 proposing armistice with Great Britain. President Wilson’s good offices requested.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (tel.)
Bulgarian note, proposing armistice with Great Britain, transmitted for communication to British Government.
From the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
Inquires whether he should accept Bulgarian note explaining policy and requesting U.S. mediation.
Message from U.S. Consul General, Sofia: Leaving by official request for Macedonian front where Bulgaria will seek arrangements for armistice.
To the Chargé in the Netherlands (tel.)
The President is willing to urge armistice upon Entente if its conditions are left for his decision.
Italy is ready to accept united command under Foch with understanding that U.S. military aid will be given.
To the Minister in Switzerland (tel.): to Murphy
Instruction to return to Sofia and take no part in Bulgarian negotiations.
Text of Bulgarian message requesting good offices of the United States in securing an armistice.
From the Consul General at Sofia (tel.)
